newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Ecopetrol says working to avoid crisis.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Ecopetrol says working to avoid crisis.

text.p: Colombia's state-run oil company Ecopetrol said Friday it was taking measures to combat the risk of a looming financial crisis highlighted earlier this week by the public finance watchdog.

The letter from Ecopetrol chief Antonio Urdinola to Comptroller General David Turbay blamed many of the problems on government fuel-pricing policy and the inflexible posture of the main oil workers' union.
However, it failed to address Turbay's criticisms of serious flaws in the company's accounting system and extra-contractual payments.
"Fortunately the national government is aware of the problems you mention," Urdinola wrote.
He said Ecopetrol was currently selling gasoline at a loss because of government-subsidized fuel prices but said he hoped the regime would be completely freed up within the next two years.

He also reiterated comments, frequently made by Ecopetrol officials, that the company has to pay too much of its operating profits into government coffers rather than reinvesting it in oil operations.
In a highly critical report issued Wednesday, Turbay said Ecopetrol made a 30.5 billion peso (about $30.5 million) operating loss in 1996 against the backdrop of a 36 percent rise in operating costs.

He said the state enterprise's net profits rose to 299.9 billion pesos last year -- 90 percent higher than the previous year -- but attributed most of that to adjustments for inflation, or monetary correction, rather than the production and sales of crude and other hydrocarbons.

In Friday's response to Turbay, Urdinola concluded by saying that as a result of a recent collective bargaining accord, Ecopetrol had set up a joint commission with the USO oil workers' union to review pension policy and consider the introduction of productivity and efficiency payments.
In 1996, Ecopetrol's bill for wage and pension payments was equivalent to 62 percent of its total revenue or about 2.5 trillion pesos.
Urdinola made no reference to some of Turbay's most stinging criticism about poor accounting procedures and the claim that the company accountant is not a qualified public accountant.
